2025_074_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC's Report to the Board of Education accompanies the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2025, with the auditor's report, management representation letter, and Government Auditing Standards letter all dated October 13, 2025. The auditors detected no misstatements, reported no disagreements with management, and noted no difficulties, while repeating an observation that the Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's three-month operating-expenditure allowance. During 2024/2025 General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $3.1 million, leaving General Fund fund balance at approximately $33.7 million, a fund balance percentage of 17.4 percent equal to roughly 9 weeks of operation.
2025_074_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_.page:
**Document type and parties**
Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC, signed by Chris Geck, CPA, covering the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025. The report is organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The auditors thank Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the business office. Key dates: engagement letter June 3, 2025; audit planning meeting June 18, 2025; auditor's report, management representation letter, and internal control/compliance letter all October 13, 2025.

**Results of the audit**
For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024 the District adopted GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the opinion is not modified with respect to the new policy. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net pension liability and OPEB net asset under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated at June 30, 2025 at $211.6 million and $36.6 million respectively, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. No misstatements were detected, no disagreements arose, no significant difficulties were encountered, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants.

**Other recommendations and observations**
The Food Service Fund's fund balance continues to exceed the USDA maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures; the District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

**Selected state funding figures cited**

| Item | Figure |
|---|---|
| 2024/2025 target foundation allowance | $9,608 per pupil |
| Public school academy target foundation, 2024/2025 | estimated $9,983 (3.9 percent increase) |
| Section 147a(4) received by the District, 2024/2025 | $5,055,278, approximately $411 per pupil |
| Statewide OPEB UAAL contribution / amount redirected | about $669 million / about $598 million |
| Section 147c(2) one-time retirement payments | $250 million |
| Section 31aa, 2024/2025 | reduced from $328 million to initially $26.5 million, plus a $125 million supplemental |
| 2026 school aid budget | $21.3 billion, about $0.5 billion higher than last year |
| 2025/2026 foundation allowance | $10,050, up from $9,608, approximately 4.6 percent |
| Section 30d state funding received, 2024/2025 | $3,719,300 |

**MPSERS plan status**
At September 30, 2024 the MPSERS net pension liability was approximately $24.5 billion, a decrease of approximately 24 percent from $32.4 billion at September 30, 2023. The net OPEB asset was approximately $4.3 billion, compared with $566 million at September 30, 2023, an increase of approximately 660 percent. The annual investment rate of return was 15.5 percent for the year ended September 30, 2024 versus 8.3 percent for the year ended September 30, 2023.

**Fund balance and other district-specific items**
General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $3.1 million in 2024/2025, reducing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33.7 million at June 30, 2025. The District's fund balance percentage is 17.4 percent, equal to approximately 9 weeks of operation; the statewide average at June 30, 2024 was approximately 24.7 percent of operating expenditures excluding transfers, equal to about a 13-week period. The District completed an arbitrage analysis and reported an arbitrage liability of $6,989,263 in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2025.

**Upcoming standards and requirements**
GASB Statement No. 103 (Financial Reporting Model Improvements) and GASB Statement No. 104 (Disclosure of Certain Capital Assets) are both effective for the District's June 30, 2026 year end. The April 2024 OMB Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit and Type A thresholds from $750,000 to $1 million, applicable for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, and raise the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000. Davis Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply to federally funded remodeling, renovation, repair, or construction contracts over $2,000.
2025_074_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC issued this Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District in connection with the audit of the School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2025. The transmittal letter is dated October 13, 2025 and thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness. The report is divided into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The Results of the Audit letter is signed by Plante & Moran, PLLC and Chris Geck, CPA.

RESPONSIBILITIES AND SCOPE. The engagement letter is dated June 3, 2025. The auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 13, 2025 addresses internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit followed the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of June 18, 2025.

SIGNIFICANT AUDIT FINDINGS. For the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2024, the School District adopted the provisions of Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences; the opinion is not modified with respect to this new accounting policy. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liability for pension and net asset for other postemployment benefits recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2025 were $211.6 million for pension and $36.6 million for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, and no misstatements were detected as a result of audit procedures. A management representation letter is dated October 13, 2025. There were no consultations with other independent accountants. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting material misstatement or inconsistency.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. The Food Service Fund's fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures. The School District should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level.

MANAGING THE CHANGING LANDSCAPE. The State did not meet its self-imposed July 1 deadline to complete the school aid budget for fiscal year 2025/2026. The May 2025 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference produced upward revisions to short- and long-term revenue growth projections for the General Fund and School Aid Fund, with cautionary notes about macroeconomic events including evolving federal trade policies. The federal One Big Beautiful Bill Act was signed on July 4, 2025 and is estimated to significantly reduce State revenue and to make Medicaid changes affecting the State budget. The U.S. Department of Education is undergoing major changes in 2025 following an executive order to dismantle it; billions of dollars in education funding were initially frozen, primarily related to Title I, and the president's budget proposal eliminates funding for Title 1-C, Title III, Title II, and Title IV-A.

2024/2025 SCHOOL FUNDING. The target foundation allowance stayed at $9,608 per pupil for public schools, while public school academies received a 3.9 percent increase estimated at $9,983. The blended pupil count used 90 percent weighting for the October 2024 count and 10 percent for the February 2024 count, with a two-year blended count available under Section 29 for districts whose 2024 final membership was lower than 2023. Under Section 147a(4), state funding historically covering the OPEB UAAL was about $669 million statewide; the 2024/2025 School Aid Bill redirected about $598 million of savings back to districts through the 147a(4) categorical, representing approximately 5.75 percent of the District's 2024 MPSERS-related payroll. For fiscal year 2024/2025 the School District received $5,055,278 under 147a(4), approximately $411 on a per pupil basis. Section 147c(2) appropriated $250 million in additional one-time payments to the retirement system, with no fund balance impact because the District was invoiced for the same amount it received. Section 147g was new in 2024/2025 and reimbursed employees for their 3 percent employer contribution to the OPEB plan, providing no additional general operating resources. GSRP funding increased, with families below four times the federal poverty level eligible for free preschool. At-risk funding is now over $1 billion. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend, and ISD Operations support continued without substantive change. The most significant reduction was mental health and school safety under Section 31aa, cut from $328 million to initially only $26.5 million on an opt-in basis, later increased by a $125 million supplemental.

2025/2026 SCHOOL FUNDING. Michigan's Legislature, split between a Republican-led House and a Democratic-led Senate, missed the July 1 statutory deadline; negotiations continued past the July 1, 2025 start of the school fiscal year and past the State's October 1, 2025 fiscal year start, forcing an emergency one-week stopgap. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act was expected to shrink Michigan's 2026 revenue by roughly $677 million if the State adopted the federal tax rule changes. The school aid budget is $21.3 billion, about $0.5 billion higher than last year, while continuing to shift approximately $1.3 billion in 2026 from the School Aid Fund to colleges and universities. Key provisions: the per pupil foundation allowance rises to $10,050 from $9,608, approximately a 4.6 percent increase; the 147a(1) MPSERS cost offset of $100 million, roughly $75 per student statewide, was eliminated; 147a(4) was completely removed compared with the 2025 budget, equating to $598 million or approximately $400 per student, reflecting the statutory reduction in the MPSERS UAAL required contribution from 20.96 percent to 15.21 percent of covered payroll; Section 30d universal free school meals continues with about $200 million; Section 31a at-risk funding increased 25 percent, adding roughly $258 million, with a new parent reporting and feedback requirement; Section 41 English Language Learner grants received a 25 percent boost to approximately $62.7 million; Section 51e foundational special education grants grew about 4 percent, roughly $25 million statewide; $65 million in one-time funds was set aside for K-3 class size reduction; Section 31aa provides over $169 million, an increase from roughly $151.5 million allocated last year including supplemental funds; and $100 million in one-time infrastructure grant funding was allocated.

LOOKING FORWARD. The State's 2026 budget is approximately $81 billion, boosting road and bridge funding by approximately $1.1 billion per year through a new 24 percent wholesale tax on marijuana producing $420 million and by replacing the 6 percent sales tax on gasoline with a 20 cents per gallon fuel tax increase, aligning with Governor Gretchen Whitmer's "fix the roads" promise; the new tax measures are expected to generate over $1.5 billion per year once fully implemented. Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, was declining by about 10,000 students per year before the pandemic, and decreased in excess of 50,000 students during the pandemic. On average it takes about 10 students to fully fund a teacher position. The next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference occurs in January 2026. The federal government missed its October 1 deadline and is in a shutdown.

MICHIGAN SCHOOL MEALS. The state-funded free breakfast and lunch initiative launched in the 2023/2024 school year under State Aid Act amendments, with Section 30d funds allocated to the Food Service Fund. For 2024/2025 the School District received $3,719,300 in Section 30d state funding. Districts apply through the Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system and must participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision, collect family income information, and write off outstanding negative student balances using resources outside the Food Service Fund. Funding continued in the 2026 state budget with a new provision allowing MDE to withhold 5 percent of state aid payments for non-adherence to federal school meal rules or failure to require completion of the federal free and reduced-price meal application.

OTHER INFORMATIONAL ITEMS. Davis Bacon prevailing wage requirements apply when federal funding is used for remodeling, renovation, repair, or construction contracts over $2,000. MPSERS, which has a September 30 year end, had a net pension liability of approximately $24.5 billion at September 30, 2024, a decrease of approximately 24 percent from $32.4 billion at September 30, 2023, and a net OPEB asset of approximately $4.3 billion compared with $566 million at September 30, 2023, an increase of approximately 660 percent; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 15.5 percent for the year ended September 30, 2024 versus 8.3 percent for the prior year. During 2024/2025 the School District's General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $3.1 million, reducing General Fund fund balance to approximately $33.7 million at June 30, 2025; the statewide average at June 30, 2024 was approximately 24.7 percent of operating expenditures excluding transfers, equal to about a 13-week period, while the School District's fund balance percentage is 17.4 percent, equal to approximately 9 weeks of operation. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, and GASB Statement No. 104, Disclosure of Certain Capital Assets, are both effective for the District's June 30, 2026 year end. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows sinking fund millages approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to be used for student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies, and equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately with annual independent audit. The District's arbitrage analysis determined an arbitrage liability of $6,989,263, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2025. The April 2024 OMB Uniform Guidance revisions increase the single audit threshold and the Type A threshold from $750,000 to $1 million, effective for fiscal year ends starting on or after October 1, 2024 and applicable for the District's fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, with new requirements beginning July 1, 2025; the equipment capitalization threshold rose from $5,000 to $10,000. Remaining items address cyber threats and the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed in October 2021, ERP marketplace changes including the sale of SchoolFinance to Linq and Skyward's marketing of Qmlative, hosting by Tyler Technologies, PowerSchool, Skyward, or an ISD, operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, artificial intelligence including Plante Moran's AI Readiness Workshops and Innovation Labs, and data analytics within K-12 districts.

2025_075_november_board_student_assessme.paragraph: "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action" is the Troy School District administration's November 2025 state assessment presentation to the Board of Education, covering M-STEP, PSAT 8, and SAT 11 results, district-by-district comparisons, and performance gaps between student groups. Troy grade 3-7 ELA proficiency was 67.9 percent in SY25 against 49.8 percent for Oakland County and 38.9 percent statewide, and grade 3-7 math was 77.9 percent against 55.4 percent and 42.7 percent. The presentation identifies special education as the largest and most persistent achievement gap while celebrating third grade ranking first in the county in both ELA and math.
2025_075_november_board_student_assessme.page:
**Purpose and framing**
Presented to the TSD Board of Education in November 2025 under the banner "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action." Stated purposes: student performance on state assessments and change over time, district-by-district performance, performance gaps between student groups, and areas of focus and celebrations. The deck notes that state assessments are summative snapshots, one part of a balanced assessment system, and are not designed to be diagnostic or to drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

**M-STEP grades 3-7, percent advanced or proficient by grade**

| Grade | ELA 2025 | ELA 2024 | Math 2025 | Math 2024 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | 67.9 | 63.2 | 77.9 | 72.4 |
| 4 | 66.3 | 66.8 | 65.9 | 68.9 |
| 5 | 67.9 | 69.0 | 65.5 | 64.1 |
| 6 | 64.5 | 64.4 | 65.8 | 66.3 |
| 7 | 66.1 | 64.8 | 68.4 | 66.0 |

**Grades 3-7 proficiency over time**

| ELA | SY19 | SY22 | SY23 | SY24 | SY25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSD | 74.0% | 69.1% | 65.9% | 63.2% | 67.9% |
| Oakland | 53.3% | 51.4% | 52.0% | 50.2% | 49.8% |
| Statewide | 45.1% | 41.6% | 40.9% | 39.6% | 38.9% |

| Math | SY19 | SY22 | SY23 | SY24 | SY25 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| TSD | 75.0% | 74.6% | 73.1% | 72.4% | 77.9% |
| Oakland | 57.3% | 53.6% | 54.8% | 55.9% | 55.4% |
| Statewide | 46.7% | 41.5% | 42.9% | 43.4% | 42.7% |

**PSAT 8 and SAT 11**
Grade 8 ELA: 84.2% in 2024 and 83.5% in 2025. Grade 11 ELA: 77.3% in 2024 and 79.3% in 2025. Grade 8 math: 64.3% in both 2024 and 2025. Grade 11 math: 59.5% in 2024 and 60.7% in 2025. Eighth grade ELA over time for TSD ran 87.1%, 81.0%, 85.6%, 84.2%, 83.5% across SY19 through SY25, against a statewide 65.3% in SY25; eighth grade math for TSD ran 75.1%, 67.5%, 69.1%, 64.3%, 64.3% against a statewide 30.4%. Eleventh grade ELA for TSD ran 82.9%, 75.3%, 76.9%, 77.3%, 79.3%, and eleventh grade math 73.6%, 61.6%, 61.3%, 59.5%, 60.7%.

**M-STEP science and social studies, grades 5, 8, 11**
Science: 61.1%, 65.3% and 50.2% in 2025 against 62.6%, 64.4% and 46.3% in 2024. Social studies: 51.0%, 68.1% and 56.9% in 2025 against 34.9%, 47.5% and 46.6% in 2024.

**Gap analysis**
Charts compare economically disadvantaged students, students with disabilities, and multilingual learners for Spring 2024 and Spring 2025. Labeled values include -27.5%, -45.7%, -34.3%, -26.4%, -45.4% and -32.7% for M-STEP 3-7 ELA and -15.3%, -18.8%, -29.6%, -33.0%, -42.6% and -44.5% for M-STEP 3-7 math. PSAT 8 ELA labels -35.3%, -52.3%, -21%, -45.0%, -21% and -44.6%; PSAT 8 math labels -25.9%, -41%, -54.1%, -55.5%, -37.9% and -27.9%; SAT 11 ELA labels -25.7%, -29.7%, -57.8%, -52.6%, -53.1% and -48.3%; SAT 11 math labels -33.8%, -39.0%, -50.8%, -51.7%, -40.5% and -40.1%.

**Celebrations and focus areas**
Third grade ranked first in the county in ELA (67.9%) and in math. Middle school honors math enrollment grew from 16% in 2021/22 to 22% in 2024/25 and 2025/26, an additional 175 middle school students annually. Troy Public Schools ranked fourth statewide in Seal of Biliteracy awards with 108. AP students scoring 3 or higher reached 89.0% in 2024-25. Focus areas are special education, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners, supported through a Multi-Tiered System of Support, Professional Learning Communities, universal supports, a district handbook, and a focus on Tier 1 instruction.
2025_075_november_board_student_assessme.verbose:
TITLE AND PURPOSE. "Pieces of One Troy: Building Belonging Through Data and Action" was presented to the Troy School District Board of Education in November 2025. The stated purposes were to review student performance on state assessments and how performance has changed over time, district-by-district performance, performance gaps between student groups, and areas of focus and celebrations. The deck cautions that state assessments are summative assessments designed to be a snapshot in time, are one part of a balanced assessment system, help policy makers and decision makers understand overall levels of achievement and identify schools, groups, and students for support, and are not designed to be diagnostic or to drive day-to-day teaching and learning.

M-STEP GRADES 3-7 BY GRADE. In ELA, percent advanced or proficient in 2025 was 67.9 in grade 3, 66.3 in grade 4, 67.9 in grade 5, 64.5 in grade 6, and 66.1 in grade 7; the 2024 figures were 63.2, 66.8, 69.0, 64.4, and 64.8. In math, 2025 figures were 77.9 in grade 3, 65.9 in grade 4, 65.5 in grade 5, 65.8 in grade 6, and 68.4 in grade 7; the 2024 figures were 72.4, 68.9, 64.1, 66.3, and 66.0.

GRADES 3-7 PROFICIENCY OVER TIME. ELA proficiency for Troy School District was 74.0% in SY19, 69.1% in SY22, 65.9% in SY23, 63.2% in SY24, and 67.9% in SY25. Oakland County was 53.3%, 51.4%, 52.0%, 50.2%, and 49.8% across the same years, and statewide was 45.1%, 41.6%, 40.9%, 39.6%, and 38.9%. Math proficiency for TSD was 75.0%, 74.6%, 73.1%, 72.4%, and 77.9%; Oakland was 57.3%, 53.6%, 54.8%, 55.9%, and 55.4%; statewide was 46.7%, 41.5%, 42.9%, 43.4%, and 42.7%.

M-STEP 3-7 COUNTY COMPARISON. The ELA grades 3-7 ranking chart lists Birmingham Public Schools, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Novi Community School District, Troy School District, Rochester Community School District, and Lake Orion Community Schools at the top, with labeled bar values of 71%, 70%, 67%, 66%, 66%, and 62%; the remainder of the county ranking runs through Clarkston Community Schools, Royal Oak Schools, Berkley School District, South Lyon Community Schools, Walled Lake Consolidated Schools, Clawson Public Schools, Avondale School District, Farmington Public School District, Huron Valley Schools, West Bloomfield School District, Oxford Community Schools, Lamphere Public Schools, Ferndale Public Schools, Brandon School District, the statewide bar, Waterford School District, Holly Area School District, Southfield Public School District, Clarenceville School District, Hazel Park, Oak Park, Madison District Public Schools, and Pontiac City School District. The math grades 3-7 ranking places Novi Community School District, Birmingham Public Schools, Troy School District, Bloomfield Hills Schools, and Rochester Community Schools at the top with labeled values of 71%, 70%, 68%, 68%, and 65%.

PSAT 8 AND SAT 11. The PSAT/SAT ELA slide reports ELA 8 at 84.2% in 2024 and 83.5% in 2025, and ELA 11 at 77.3% in 2024 and 79.3% in 2025. The math slide reports Math 8 at 64.3% in both 2024 and 2025, and Math 11 at 59.5% in 2024 and 60.7% in 2025. Eighth grade proficiency over time in ELA: TSD 87.1% in SY19, 81.0% in SY22, 85.6% in SY23, 84.2% in SY24, and 83.5% in SY25; Oakland 72.5%, 69.5%, 71.4%, 74.4%, and 74.5%; statewide 61.9%, 59.7%, 59.7%, 64.5%, and 65.3%. Eighth grade math over time: TSD 75.1%, 67.5%, 69.1%, 64.3%, and 64.3%; Oakland 55.1%, 47.6%, 49.0%, 45.9%, and 42.4%; statewide 41.4%, 36.2%, 36.3%, 32.6%, and 30.4%. Eleventh grade ELA over time: TSD 82.9%, 75.3%, 76.9%, 77.3%, and 79.3%; Oakland 63.1%, 59.5%, 59.5%, 60.0%, and 64.1%; statewide 55.3%, 51.6%, 52.2%, 51.3%, and 55.4%. Eleventh grade math over time: TSD 73.6%, 61.6%, 61.3%, 59.5%, and 60.7%; Oakland 46.5%, 39.4%, 39.1%, 35.6%, and 37.4%; statewide 36.3%, 30.0%, 29.9%, 26.3%, and 27.5%.

COUNTY COMPARISONS FOR PSAT 8 AND SAT 11. The PSAT 8 ELA county chart labels Bloomfield Hills Schools, Berkley School District, Birmingham Public Schools, Rochester Community Schools, Novi Community School District, and Troy School District at 89%, 89%, 89%, 88%, 85%, and 83%, with the statewide bar at 65%. The PSAT 8 math county chart labels Bloomfield Hills Schools, Troy School District, Birmingham Public Schools, Novi Community School District, and Rochester Community Schools at 70%, 64%, 64%, 63%, and 60%, with statewide at 30%. The SAT Evidence Based Reading and Writing grade 11 chart labels Novi Community School District, Birmingham Public Schools, Bloomfield Hills Schools, Rochester Community School District, Troy School District, and South Lyon Community Schools at 85.1, 82.5, 82.3, 81.8, 79.3, and 75.6, with statewide at 55.4. The SAT Math grade 11 chart labels Novi Community School District, Troy School District, Birmingham Public Schools, Rochester Community School District, and Bloomfield Hills Schools at 64.7, 60.7, 58.9, 56.6, and 56.5, with statewide at 27.5.

M-STEP SCIENCE AND SOCIAL STUDIES. For grades 5, 8, and 11, science percent advanced or proficient was 61.1%, 65.3%, and 50.2% in 2025 against 62.6%, 64.4%, and 46.3% in 2024. Social studies was 51.0%, 68.1%, and 56.9% in 2025 against 34.9%, 47.5%, and 46.6% in 2024.

GAP ANALYSIS. The implications slide states that districts have historically struggled to raise the performance of students with disabilities, economically disadvantaged students, and English learners on par with countywide and statewide rates, a phenomenon commonly known as the Performance Gap and also referred to as an Opportunity Gap. The Multi-Tiered System of Support slide lists district commitment to building coherence in process, focus on systems that support all students, commitment to Professional Learning Communities in process at all schools, universal supports, review of progress monitoring of any student on a plan, development of a district handbook, interventions taught by content strong teachers, and focus on Tier 1 instruction. Gap charts compare Spring 2024 with Spring 2025 for economically disadvantaged students, students with disabilities, and multilingual learners. The M-STEP grades 3-7 ELA chart carries labels of -27.5%, -45.7%, -34.3%, -26.4%, -45.4%, and -32.7%. The M-STEP grades 3-7 math chart carries labels of -15.3%, -18.8%, -29.6%, -33.0%, -42.6%, and -44.5%. The PSAT 8 ELA gap chart carries labels of -35.3%, -52.3%, -21%, -45.0%, -21%, and -44.6%. The PSAT 8 math gap chart carries labels of -25.9%, -41%, -54.1%, -55.5%, -37.9%, and -27.9%. The SAT 11 ELA gap chart carries labels of -25.7%, -29.7%, -57.8%, -52.6%, -53.1%, and -48.3%. The SAT 11 math gap chart carries labels of -33.8%, -39.0%, -50.8%, -51.7%, -40.5%, and -40.1%.

ANALYSIS. Strengths listed: TSD consistently outperforms county and state averages, demonstrating strong and effective instructional practices; all subgroups (economically disadvantaged, special education, English learners) are performing above their statewide peers, indicating effective support systems; performance stability over three years underscores resilience and sustainability of current practices; and third grade is first in the county in ELA and math. Focus areas for continuous improvement: special education, described as the largest and most persistent achievement gap, addressed through inclusive practices with a focus on Tier 1 instruction and targeted interventions provided by content strong teachers; economically disadvantaged students, who outperform state and county peers but of whom fewer than half meet proficiency; and English learners, who perform strongly compared with county and state peers but for whom a performance gap remains and ongoing language acquisition and academic language development support is essential.

MIDDLE SCHOOL MATH. Cohort performance slides cover the current 9th grade Class of 2029, described as the last split cohort with the 6/7 and 7/8 track and IM 6/7 and the first cohort with a choice after 7th grade of Honors Algebra 1, and the current 8th grade Class of 2030, described as IM 6th/IM 7th. Displayed cohort percentages include 65%, 63%, 68%, 68%, 62%, 65%, 66%, and 65%. Middle school honors math enrollment by year: the percentage of middle school students enrolled in Honors Algebra 1 was 13.1% in 2021-2022, 12.7% in 2022-2023, 12.0% in 2023-2024, 19.8% in 2024-2025, and 17.3% in 2025-2026; Honors Geometry was 2.08%, 1.66%, 1.87%, 1.30%, and 2.93%; Honors Algebra 2 was 0.81%, 0.76%, 0.20%, 1.10%, and 1.90%. The narrative states that middle school enrollment in honors math has increased by 6%, growing from 16% in 2021/22 to 22% in 2024/25 and 2025/26, representing an additional 175 middle school students annually in 2024/25 and 2025/26 enrolled in honors level math.

THIRD GRADE ELA AND OTHER CELEBRATIONS. The Spring 2025 third grade ELA proficiency county chart places Troy School District first at 67.9%, followed by Birmingham Public Schools at 66.6%, Bloomfield Hills Schools at 65.6%, Novi Community School District at 63.1%, Rochester Community School District at 61.6%, Lake Orion Community Schools at 61.5%, Clarkston Community School District at 58.6%, and continuing through 54.1%, 51.3%, 50.5%, 48.7%, 48.4%, 48.1%, 47.3%, 45.9%, 44.9%, 42.7%, 41.6%, 40.6%, 39.6%, a statewide bar at 38.9%, then 37.0%, 34.8%, 33.8%, and 21.0%. TSD third grade math is also reported first in the county. 2025_079_2_b_troy_school_district_transp.paragraph: School Bus Logistics, LLC prepared this bell time study executive summary for Troy School District, dated 4/24/25, Version 1.0, evaluating four scenarios that each incorporate a later start time for all high school students. Against a 2024-2025 baseline of 32 general education vehicles, 153 daily labor hours, and 1,161 daily miles, Scenario A would require 39 vehicles, Scenario B 43 vehicles, and Scenario C 56 vehicles under a 2-tier hybrid system. The board decided not to proceed with combining middle and high school students on the same bus, and the node-stop variation in Scenario D was not pursued because it did not reduce the number of vehicles required.
2025_079_2_b_troy_school_district_transp.page:
**Document and parties**
Bell Time Study executive summary from School Bus Logistics, LLC (SBL), dated 4/24/25, Version 1.0, prepared for Troy School District. The cover letter dated Thursday, April 24, 2025 is addressed to Dan Trudel, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and signed by Timothy Micheals, Route Logistics Consultant, who can be reached at 331-575-2453 or tim.micheals@schoolbuslogistics.com. The letter also thanks Kathy for collaboration throughout the process.

**Objectives and methodology**
Objectives were to assess the current fleet schedule to establish a baseline, develop route packages aligned with bell time options for each scenario, and ensure each scenario incorporates a later high school start time. For each scenario SBL provides proposed bell times including AM arrivals and PM departures, analysis of vehicle requirements, daily driver hours, and daily vehicle mileage. SBL used Versatrans RP routing software focused on general education transportation, with all data housed on Troy School District servers and accessed via secure remote connection. Data verification and cleanup addressed anchor sit times, stop sit times, and student load times. Baseline documentation criteria were service windows at schools, total number of eligible riders, actual load counts provided by the district, and current route pairings.

**Baseline, SY 24-25**
Five-tier system. Tier 1 Athens HS and Troy HS: 7:20:00 AM bell, 2:08:00 PM bell, 06:48 instructional minutes, 2:17:00 PM departure, 9 and 20 buses. Tier 2 Larson MS and Boulan MS: 7:52:00 AM, 2:40:00 PM, 06:48, 2:45:00 PM, 9 and 14 buses. Tier 3 Baker MS and Smith MS: 8:17:00 AM, 3:05:00 PM, 06:48, 3:10:00 PM, 9 and 11 buses. Tier 4 Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, and Wattles elementaries: 8:39:00 AM, 3:37:00 PM, 06:58, 3:44:00 PM. Tier 5 Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard elementaries: 9:09:00 AM, 4:07:00 PM, 06:58, 4:14:00 PM. Baseline totals: 32 vehicles for Gen Ed routing on the current 5-tier system, daily labor hours of 153, daily mileage of 1161.

**Scenario results**

| Scenario | Description | Vehicles | Daily labor hours | Daily mileage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline | Current 5-tier | 32 | 153 | 1161 |
| A (Task 1) | High school time shift, 7:00 AM to 8:00 AM arrival | 39 (7 additional) | 197 | 1161 |
| B (Task 2) | Elementary and middle school switch | 43 (11 additional) | 215 | 1161 |
| C (Task 3) | Middle/high school combination, 2-tier hybrid | 56 (24 additional) | 181 | 1387 |
| D (Task 4) | Node stops variation of Scenario A | estimated 37-39 (5-7 additional) | estimated 197 | estimated 1161 |

**Scenario notes**
In Scenario A, Boulan Park and Larson move to a 7:00 AM arrival and Baker and Smith shift to 7:30 AM, with elementary arrivals unchanged. Scenario B reversed the middle school and elementary tiers and was determined not feasible because of the required increase in vehicle count and the potential for creating latchkey situations for elementary students. In Scenario C, Larsen and Baker Middle School students were paired with Athens High School students and Boulan Park and Smith Middle School students with Troy High School students; a 4-tier hybrid option that could reduce the fleet to an estimated 37-39 buses was briefly explored, but the school board decided not to proceed with combining middle and high school students on the same bus. Scenario D consolidated stops using Troy and Athens High Schools as a sample, showing 50 stops being removed from those routes; savings would be in mileage and fuel reductions, labor time would have minimal reductions due to driver guarantees, and route time savings would be in deadhead time between runs. Because it did not reduce the number of vehicles required, Scenario D was not pursued further.
2025_079_2_b_troy_school_district_transp.verbose:
OVERVIEW. School Bus Logistics, LLC (SBL) produced this Bell Time Study executive summary for Troy School District, dated 4/24/25 and marked Version 1.0. The transmittal letter, dated Thursday, April 24, 2025, is addressed to Dan Trudel, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, and signed by Timothy Micheals, Route Logistics Consultant, who lists a contact number of 331-575-2453 and an email address of tim.micheals@schoolbuslogistics.com. The letter thanks Mr. Trudel and Kathy for their collaboration and states that the report provides a comprehensive analysis of four distinct scenarios focusing on the impact of each scenario and the additional vehicle requirements.

STUDY OVERVIEW AND OBJECTIVES. SBL was selected to conduct a bell time study evaluating four distinct scenarios. At the request of the school board, each scenario includes a later start time for all high school students. Project objectives were to assess the current fleet schedule to establish a baseline, develop route packages aligned with bell time options for each scenario, and ensure each scenario incorporates a later high school start time. For each scenario, SBL provides proposed bell times including AM arrivals and PM departures, an analysis of vehicle requirements, daily driver hours associated with each route package, and daily vehicle mileage for each route package.

METHODOLOGY. SBL used Versatrans RP routing software to develop route sets for each scenario, focusing on general education transportation. All data was housed on Troy School District's servers, and SBL accessed it via a secure remote connection to compile and analyze results within Versatrans RP. SBL first established a baseline reflecting the current routing structure and configuration of route packages. Data verification and cleanup were required before in-depth analysis, addressing elements such as anchor sit times, stop sit times, and student load times. The finalized baseline data was documented using service windows at schools for unloading and loading, total number of eligible riders reflecting utilization of seat capacity, actual load counts provided by Troy School District, and current route pairings.

BASELINE DATA, SY 24-25. The analysis is based on data from the 2024-2025 school year. The baseline bell time table lists tier, school, AM arrival, AM bell time, PM bell time, instructional minutes in HH:MM, PM departure, and number of buses. Tier 1: Athens HS, arrival 6:48 to 7:10, bell 7:20:00 AM, PM bell 2:08:00 PM, 06:48 instructional minutes, departure 2:17:00 PM, 9 buses; Troy HS, arrival 6:55 to 7:05, bell 7:20:00 AM, 2:08:00 PM, 06:48, 2:17:00 PM, 20 buses. Tier 2: Larson MS, arrival 7:25 to 7:50, bell 7:52:00 AM, 2:40:00 PM, 06:48, 2:45:00 PM, 9 buses; Boulan MS, arrival 7:19 to 7:45, same bells, 14 buses. Tier 3: Baker MS, arrival 7:50 to 8:10, bell 8:17:00 AM, 3:05:00 PM, 06:48, 3:10:00 PM, 9 buses; Smith MS, arrival 7:51 to 8:10, same bells, 11 buses. Tier 4: Bemis ES arrival 8:20:00 AM (7 buses), Hill ES 8:35:00 AM (1 bus), Martell ES 8:24:00 AM (7 AM/8 PM), Troy Union ES 8:25:00 AM (7 buses), and Wattles ES 8:24:00 AM (7 buses), all with an 8:39:00 AM bell, 3:37:00 PM PM bell, 06:58 instructional minutes, and 3:44:00 PM departure. Tier 5: Barnard ES 9:00:00 AM (4 buses), Costello ES 8:55:00 AM (3 buses, 4:17:00 PM departure), Morse ES 9:00:00 AM (5 buses), Hamilton ES 9:03:00 AM (6 AM/5 PM), Schroeder ES 9:05:00 AM (7 buses), and Leonard ES 8:52:00 AM (5 buses), all with a 9:09:00 AM bell, 4:07:00 PM PM bell, 06:58 instructional minutes, and 4:14:00 PM departure. Baseline results: 32 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the current 5-tier system, with daily labor hours of 153 and daily mileage of 1161.

TASK 1 - SCENARIO A (HIGH SCHOOL TIME SHIFT). SBL explored shifting the current high school arrival time from 7:00 AM to 8:00 AM. Under this scenario, Boulan Park and Larson would move to a 7:00 AM arrival while Baker and Smith would shift to 7:30 AM, and elementary school arrival times would remain unchanged. Fleet schedule pairings were modified while maintaining the existing routing structure. The Scenario A bell time table places Larson MS and Boulan MS in Tier 1 with a 7:00:00 AM arrival, 7:20:00 AM bell, 2:08:00 PM PM bell, 6:48:00 instructional minutes, and 2:17:00 PM departure, at 9 and 14 buses; Baker MS and Smith MS in Tier 2 with a 7:30:00 AM arrival, 7:52:00 AM bell, 2:40:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 2:47:00 PM departure, at 9 and 11 buses; Athens HS and Troy HS in Tier 3 with an 8:00:00 AM arrival, 8:17:00 AM bell, 3:05:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:10:00 PM departure, at 9 and 20 buses; and the Tier 4 and Tier 5 elementary schedules unchanged from baseline. Results: 39 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 5-tier system, described as 7 additional vehicles, with daily labor hours of 197 and daily mileage of 1161.

TASK 2 - SCENARIO B (ELEMENTARY AND MIDDLE SCHOOL SWITCH). Scenario B used the route set from Scenario A with the primary adjustment being the reversal of the middle school and elementary school tiers. After review and discussion between SBL and the Troy School District, it was determined that this scenario was not feasible; the required increase in vehicle count and the potential for creating latchkey situations for elementary students presented significant challenges. Fleet schedule pairings were modified to reflect the proposed tier shift while the existing routing remained unchanged. The Scenario B table puts Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard elementaries in Tier 1 with a 7:00:00 AM arrival, 7:10:00 AM bell, 2:08:00 PM PM bell, 6:58:00 instructional minutes, and 2:17:00 PM departure; Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, and Wattles in Tier 2 with a 7:30:00 AM arrival, 7:42:00 AM bell, 2:40:00 PM, 6:58:00, and 2:47:00 PM departure; Athens HS and Troy HS in Tier 3 with an 8:00:00 AM arrival, 8:17:00 AM bell, 3:05:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:10:00 PM departure at 9 and 20 buses; Larson MS and Boulan MS in Tier 4 with an 8:30:00 AM arrival, 8:49:00 AM bell, 3:37:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:44:00 PM departure at 9 and 14 buses; and Baker MS and Smith MS in Tier 5 with a 9:00:00 AM arrival, 9:19:00 AM bell, 4:07:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 4:14:00 PM departure at 9 and 11 buses. Results: 43 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 5-tier system, described as 11 additional vehicles, with daily labor hours of 215 and daily mileage of 1161.

TASK 3 - SCENARIO C (MIDDLE / HIGH SCHOOL COMBINATION). Scenario C was developed in response to feedback from the Troy School District and involved combining middle and high school students on the same bus routes, increasing the eligible rider load per vehicle. Larsen and Baker Middle School students were paired with Athens High School students, while Boulan Park and Smith Middle School students were paired with Troy High School students. New route sets were created and routing criteria adjusted to accommodate the combined student populations, with new routes developed to transport students to and from multiple schools on a single bus. In the Scenario C table, Tier 1 includes Larson MS, Baker MS, and Athens HS marked "Shared / 24" and Boulan MS, Smith MS, and Troy HS marked "Shared / 37"; the middle schools have a 7:30:00 AM arrival, 7:52:00 AM bell, 2:40:00 PM PM bell, 6:48:00 instructional minutes, and 2:47:00 PM departure, while the high schools have an 8:00:00 AM arrival, 8:17:00 AM bell, 3:05:00 PM, 6:48:00, and 3:10:00 PM departure. Tier 2 places all eleven elementaries (Bemis, Hill, Martell, Troy Union, Wattles, Barnard, Costello, Morse, Hamilton, Schroeder, and Leonard) at an 8:30:00 AM arrival, 8:39:00 AM bell, 3:37:00 PM, 6:58:00, and 3:44:00 PM departure. Results: 56 vehicles are required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 2-tier hybrid system, described as 24 additional vehicles, with daily labor hours of 181 and daily mileage of 1387. An option to implement a 4-tier hybrid system that would stagger drop-off and pickup times was briefly explored and had the potential to reduce the number of vehicles needed to an estimated 37-39 buses; however, when this scenario was presented to the school board, a decision was made not to proceed with combining middle and high school students on the same bus, and the option was set aside.

TASK 4 - SCENARIO D (NODE STOPS). Scenario D was developed as a variation of Scenario A focused on a node-based stop system using strategically placed neighborhood-based stops, aiming to consolidate bus stops and increase walking distances for high school students to reduce the number of individual stops. The node-based consolidation reduced total mileage but did not decrease driver labor hours, and similar outcomes would be expected if applied to the elementary and middle school tiers. Because the option did not reduce the number of vehicles required, it was not pursued further. SBL used Troy and Athens High Schools as a sample for node-based stop consolidation, counting only stops with assigned students. Sample route data includes AHS AM 01 with 62 assigned students, 5 total stops, 2 removed, 3 remaining; AHS AM 03 with 104 students, 10 stops, 2 removed, 8 remaining; AHS AM 11 with 58 students, 6 stops, 1 removed, 5 remaining; AHS AM 12 with 78 students, 7 stops, 1 removed, 6 remaining; AHS AM 17 with 65 students, 11 stops, 4 removed, 7 remaining; AHS AM 22 with 99 students, 9 stops, 3 removed, 6 remaining; AHS AM 25 with 72 students, 10 stops, 4 removed, 6 remaining; AHS AM 26 with 59 students, 7 stops, 1 removed, 6 remaining; and AHS AM 49 with 75 students, 5 stops, 0 removed, 5 remaining. Troy High routes include THS AM 04 (65 students, 6 stops, 3 removed, 3 remaining), THS AM 05 (72 students, 7 stops, 2 removed, 5 remaining, order changed), THS AM 07 (43 students, 10 stops, 1 removed, 9 remaining), THS AM 08 (55 students, 5 stops, 1 removed, 4 remaining, two stops combined at MOR), THS AM 09 (79 students, 5 stops, 1 removed, 4 remaining), THS AM 10 (46 students, 7 stops, 0 removed, 7 remaining, hazard stops that cannot be consolidated due to safety), THS AM 14 (91 students, 6 stops, 0 removed, 6 remaining, could consolidate 2), THS AM 16 (87 students, 10 stops, 3 removed, 7 remaining), THS AM 19 (47 students, 2 stops, 0 removed, 2 remaining, MOR overflow), THS AM 20 (88 students, 7 stops, 3 removed, 4 remaining), THS AM 23 (64 students, 13 stops, 1 removed, 12 remaining), THS AM 24 (73 students, 8 stops, 2 removed, 6 remaining), THS AM 28 (94 students, 9 stops, 4 removed, 5 remaining), THS AM 31 (57 students, 5 stops, 0 removed, 5 remaining), THS AM 32 (111 students, 11 stops, 2 removed, 9 remaining), THS AM 34 (60 students, 6 stops, 1 removed, 5 remaining), THS AM 35 (91 students, 10 stops, 4 removed, 6 remaining), THS AM 46 (72 students, 7 stops, 1 removed, 6 remaining), THS AM 52 (82 students, 9 stops, 1 removed, 8 remaining), and THS AM 53 (68 students, 8 stops, 2 removed, 6 remaining). The Task 4 summary shows 50 stops being removed from Athens and Troy High School routes; savings would be in the form of mileage and fuel reductions, labor time would have minimal reductions due to driver guarantees, and route time savings would be in the form of deadhead time between runs. Scenario D is summarized as an estimated 37-39 vehicles required for Gen Ed routing utilizing the 5-tier system (5-7 additional vehicles), with estimated daily labor hours of 197 and estimated daily mileage of 1161.

CONCLUSION. The report states that all scenarios explore later start times for high school students but each carries distinct trade-offs in fleet utilization, driver hours, and overall efficiency. School Bus Logistics states its commitment to supporting Troy School District in balancing student well-being, operational feasibility, and community needs while focusing on safety, and invites follow-up questions or further analysis.
